html:
Directory on the Oratory

Introduction

Our Constitutions affirm that “the oratory is still relevant”1; it is understood, by what was said immediately before, that it treats of the Oratory “according to the spirit of Saint Philip Neri and Saint John Bosco.”2 It was the first educational institute of the latter and the one of greatest apostolic importance.3

In this directory we want to focus on that which we understand to be the two principal forms of the oratory: the one, in the strict sense, is the Oratory as Institution; the other, in the broader sense, is identified with the “oratorian spirit.”

Part I: The Oratory

Chapter 1: Nature

The festive oratory4, is a religiously fervent and morally healthy environment that surrounds the youth in his totality so as to orient him towards possessing the heavenly life in a climate of religiosity, of reasonable amiability, joy, and freedom and youthful expansion.5

The first Oratory of St. John Bosco in Valdoco was for youth:

House, that welcomes and provides accommodations

Parish, that transmits the Gospel

School, accessible to those who in other places would have difficulties

Patio, where one shares joy and friendship.

It is a form of human and Christian preservation, redemption, and salvation of youth, especially the abandoned; that is, it should fulfill the function of an integral educative environment that includes all of the youth, who should find the possibility of a development of his qualities and interests. It is an authentic form of education.

The end of the Oratory is to form “good Christians and honest citizens.”6

Chapter 2: Importance

St John Bosco said: “Only in this way can one radically do the good for the population of a place...”7

This is an apostolate of extraordinary importance, since for some youth it will be the only “voice” of salvation.8

Every superior should try to organize a festive oratory in his parish, school, house, and other works under his jurisdiction, considering that this work is one of the most important of all those that have been entrusted to him. “It is the only form of complete Christian education accessible to great numbers of youth.”9 The oratory is an initial fount of vocations.

Chapter 3: Ends of the Oratory

The function of the festive oratory, as described in the first article of the Rule that St. John Bosco wrote for his oratories: “the end of the festive Oratory is, after attending the sacred functions of the Church, to entertain youth on feast days with enjoyable amusements.”10 That is to say:

To entertain the youth on feast days, because we are especially considering working youth, those who, especially on feast days, are exposed to great moral and corporal dangers; but this is not to exclude the students who want to attend the feast days or vacations.

With enjoyable and honest amusements, really able to amuse and not to tire. Above all, games, amusements, or whatever other manner of recreation that may compromise the health or morality of the youth must not be allowed.

After attending the sacred functions of the Church, because religious instruction is of primary importance: the rest is accidental and only an incentive for attracting the youth.11

Chapter 4: The Environment of the Oratory

The oratory is fundamentally an environment, a climate, an atmosphere, that we can characterize through different aspects:

An educative environment

A religious environment

An environment that is open to all

An environment of joy and freedom

An environment of charity

An environment of family

The Oratory should be like a prolongation of the family and of the Church, for the family is, as St. Thomas teaches, like “a spiritual womb.”12 Because just as in the physical womb each human receives life, love, protection, care, development, food, etc., so also, in the family life must continue to be generated and conserved. There he receives love and education, is joyful and protected, learns to practice all virtues, relates oneself to others, etc. This is how the Oratory should be.

Moreover, the Church itself is considered a “spiritual womb” that continues to generate men. St. Thomas, commenting on the Gospel of St. John, speaks of spiritual rebirth, because man, aged spiritually by sin, can be renewed through the help of grace: “he can, in a higher way, enter into the spiritual womb, that is to say, the Church, through the sacrament of Baptism.”13

Because of this, the true Oratory should be like a “spiritual womb” where the children and youth should continue their integral growth.

It is this spirit that must inform all the activities of the Oratory. It deals with living Christianity in its fullness, with having the same spirit that Christ had in each moment, with making of the life of the Oratory “like a new Incarnation of the Word.”14

Every true Christian should know how to surround himself with an environment where he lives in “righteousness, peace, and joy in the holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:7). Following the counsels of the great pedagogue and creator of the Festive Oratory, St. John Bosco, we consider that the spirit of the Oratory consists in creating an environment of education, religious, and love15, in a climate of friendship.

Article 1: Educative Environment

This environment always must be educative, in that it should teach man the true and authentic way to live; for this reason, in the same way that it takes responsibility that the religious life – since this is the foundation of man’s life, and that which informs all of man – produces an education for all the activities of life.

Since the Oratory has the function of integral educative environment, it must embrace the whole human person during the whole day, offer the possibility of a complete and harmonious development of the youth’s qualities and interests.

Precisely because it is an essential, religiously educative and fundamentally Christian environment, the Oratory becomes a school of instruction, of religious practice, and of Christian inspiration of life.

The true climate of every Oratory must have as its foundation the integral, corrective, curative and constructive educative function. It is moreover an integral and profound form of education. It is not a substitution, not a lesser evil, not a form of transition or like a “diminutive” educative institution, but rather like a more complete Christian form of education accessible to great masses youth.

The Oratory is a spirit that must have continuity, in such a way that it should live not only on feast days, but rather also during the whole week and in each moment of the day.

Article 2: Religious Environment

The principal end of this work is the supernatural one. The oratory climate must bring us to grow in the practice of the theological virtues and above all in charity, queen of all virtues; it is she that is the essential constitutive element of every authentic Oratory. In a special way it must manifest this spirit in religious practices, above all in the Mass, in adoration, in the main prayers, in get-togethers, entertainment, and healthy recreation.

Without the religious element, all our activities are a waste of time: If the Lord does not build the house, in vain do its builders labor; if the Lord does not watch over the city, in vain does the watchman keep vigil (Ps 127:1). Not just the important and transcendent works but also the gatherings, entertainment, outings and even sports should be infused with the religious spirit – they make no sense simply as such, but only in the proper ordering of each one of these activities to the first and principal end that they have, that is: to have us grow in the love of God above all things and of our neighbor as ourselves.

One who considers the Oratory merely as a kind of free time, a place of recreation, or a cheerful meeting place for youth would falsify what the authentic Oratory wants to be. It is much more than this, for all these activities are designed to bring the participants to grow in the spiritual life. Without this aspect they become a lamentable waste of time.

In the oratorian climate each one ought to “work in every way possible to infuse into the hearts of the youth the love of God, respect for sacred things, the value of frequenting the sacraments, a filial devotion to the Blessed Virgin, and all that constitutes true piety.”16 This fruitful environment will not be achieved if it is not supported by or built on true piety and the practice of Christian virtues.

In order for the environment of religious practice to be foundational, frequenting the sacraments of Confession17 and Eucharist must be insisted upon. “Frequent confession and communion and daily Mass are the columns that must sustain the educational edifice if intimidation and the stick are to be kept far away.”18 “Remember that the first method of education is good confessions and good communions.”19 The Oratory should be a place where all “… can have the convenience to fulfill their religious duties and, at the same time, receive instruction, orientation, and advice, so as to direct their life in a Christian and honest manner.”20

Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All

All need to save their soul and body. The Oratory must be universal, like the salvific will of God. The student should be surrounded by a constant, kind, and solicitous assistance. The Oratory must be open to all. It should take into account all the values of the youth and of all.

“The festive Oratory of Don Bosco is an institution totally his, that differs from whatever other similar institution as much as by the end that it pursues as by the means that it uses. According to Don Bosco, the Oratory is not for a determined category of youth in preference to others, but for all without distinction, from the age of seven up; there is no impediment stemming from the family situation or from the parents’ presentation of the youth: the only condition to be admitted is to come with a good will to have fun, be instructed, and to fulfill with all the others their religious duties. The cause of a youth’s expulsion from the Oratory can neither be the vivacity of his temperament, nor the occasional rebellion, nor the lack of education, nor what ever juvenile defect caused by frivolity or natural stubbornness; but only systematic and contagious insubordination, blasphemy, bad conversations and scandal. With the exception of these cases, the tolerance of the director should be unlimited. All the youth, especially the most abandoned and miserable, must understand that the Oratory is for them the paternal house, the refuge, the ark of salvation, the secure way to become better under the transforming action of the affection of the Director, more than his paternity.”21

The Oratory does not have schedules; it should fill to the brim the free hours of a youth’s life, “to saturate it with possibilities, with joy, with human and heavenly values, with formation and fun, with instruction and edification.”22 The Oratory tends to prolong itself, in one way or another, throughout the week.23

All have the right to receive moral and religious assistance: “However, the poor, most abandoned and most ignorant are admitted and attended to preferentially, because they have the most need of assistance in order to maintain themselves in the way of eternal salvation.”24 “To entertain the most abandoned youth,”25 repeats Don Bosco in his Memoirs.

The conditions for acceptance are broad: “All are free to frequent this Oratory. But all must submit themselves to the orders of those in charge and observe the proper behavior in recreation, in the church, and outside the Oratory.”26

“The boy that enters the Oratory should be persuaded that this is a place of religion, where we desire to form good Christians and honest citizens. For this reason it is rigorously prohibited to blaspheme or to have conversations against good customs or against the Holy Catholic religion. Whoever commits one of these faults will be paternally warned the first time, and if he does not amend, the Director will be notified, who will expel him from the Oratory…. Disobedient youth can also be admitted, provided that they do not give scandal and that they manifest the will to better their conduct.”27

The Oratory is a complete program of material help and family support, of evangelization and of conviviality, of culture and of mission, finally, a community where one can be with friends and be happy.

Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom

The festive Oratory is a “free” educative system in which the obligation and regulation are substituted by the attraction of the festive environment and of charity. An environment of novelty and joyful saturation of the youth should be created through games28: “a diversity of games according to the ages of the children and the customs of the place is recommended – these constitute one of the most efficacious means of attracting the youth to the Oratory. It helps encourage frequent attendance and good behavior at the festive Oratories if prizes are distributed at determined times, for example, books, objects of devotion, clothing; as well as lotteries, outings, skits and moral plays, music classes, little parties, etc.”29 The activities that can be carried out in the Oratory should not only be amusing, but also, when possible, they should be constructive.

Joy is essential to the spirit of the Oratory. The Christian life is to prepare for a feast, and to live the heavenly feast while still on earth. Joy springs from possessing that which it loves. One is truly joyful when one is joyful in love: “where charity rejoices, there is festivity.”30 And this is because every feast implies a existential richness that in its turn is born of a renunciation, for one cannot have a time of feasting if one has not denied oneself something. And this renunciation implies love, for there is no renunciation where there is no love.31 Don Bosco saw in dreams how the spirit of long ago had decayed: “shouts and songs of jubilation are not heard”32 from which “the coldness in many when approaching the holy sacraments originates, and negligence in the practices of piety in the church and outside of it…”33

Freedom has its source in charity as well, therefore if we surrender our heart to Love Himself, nothing an no one can impede us from coming to be with the Lord, for we are no longer two but one: What will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or anguish, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? … No, in all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through Him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor present things, nor future things, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:35, 37-39). Love is that to which we are called and in what we find true freedom, not carnal freedom: For you were called to freedom, brothers. But do not use this freedom as an opportunity for the flesh; rather, serve one another through love. For the whole law is fulfilled in one statement, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal 5:13-14). It is the freedom of the one who, solely for love of God and of neighbor, does good and avoids evil.

In our oratories there should not be a vigilance of the police type, but rather a paternal watchfulness, for all the members of our Religious Family are none other than children of God, who rejoice in the freedom proper to the children of God, because to rejoice in freedom, Christ set us free (Gal 5:1). The spirit of family that is instilled in our oratories lives in a climate of freedom.

The Oratory is of itself a “fragile” institution, since its attendance is totally free – it is based on voluntary attendance. This voluntary aspect has a most important role: “this voluntary aspect is that which makes the action of the leaders much more varied, elastic, dynamic, and rich in initiatives, so that they are not limited to waiting and receiving, but like Don Bosco, organize “raids” of collection, true peaceful “searches” (in city squares, streets, bars, neighborhoods, etc.).34

“Making festive each Sunday at the Oratory should be one of the most elemental preoccupations of the educators that work in it.” The variety that attracts and enthuses the youth should be a great preoccupation: “in this is the whole secret and the success of the Oratory. When a Director is not able, with holy industries, to make festive the Sundays of his Oratory or, when, even having great plans, does not know how to communicate them to his assistants, except in spurts and only at the time of putting them into effect, then the Oratory will become a little Babel and the youth will begin to be tired and stop coming.”35

Article 5: Environment of Charity

The life of the Oratory should be interwoven with the Christian virtues of piety and joy, but above all the divine and human bond that establishes charity and true love must exist. Charity should pedagogically be transformed into “amorevolezza,” as St. John Bosco masterfully teaches. Charity should always appear, become visible, transform into a human means of attraction and conquest.36

The spirit of our communities must be founded in charity that be transformed, as Don Bosco says, into “amorevolezza.” This is a typical expression of the saint, that does not have a satisfactory translation in English and that signifies: kindness, love, the affection of a father or older brother. This “amorevolezza” is described perfectly in the Circular Letter on Punishments, a quote that can be analogically applied to every religious: “Before all, if we want to present ourselves as friends of the authentic good of all our students, if we want to oblige them to fulfill their duties, we should never forget that we represent the parents of these beloved youth…. If then you have to be true parents of your students, it is necessary that you have the hearts of parents and never use repression and punishment without reason;” and further on, “Stay firm in looking for good and in preventing evil; be, nevertheless, always gentle and prudent. Be persevering and kind, and you will see how God will make you lords over the least docile hearts…” Remember the religious that “over all must be mother since she bears children by the cross, by prayer, by apostolic zeal, by example, and by announcement.”37 The saint finishes by recalling that the work is God’s: “remember that education is the business of hearts and that God is the Lord of the hearts. We can do nothing if God does not teach us the art and we do not put the keys in His hand.”38

Every community will really be such if they live the words of St. Paul: Charity is patient and kind…. It bears all things, hopes all things, believes all things, endures all things (1 Cor 13:4, 7). The effectiveness of this life is that it always has a spirit of sacrifice, a great patience, charity, benevolence towards all, “works, community duties, contradictions… harshness, all these are little to her who immolates herself with generosity and unlimited confidence in God.”39 All in them must be expressed in the language of love, including punishments themselves. Through charity we show our knowledge of and desire to unite ourselves with God Who has first loved us.40

To achieve this environment of charity it is necessary that the students not only be loved but also feel love. On this the saintly pedagogue insisted frequently; in writing to the directors he described a dream he had and said that in their Oratories the best is lacking: love, in such a way “that the youth be not only loved but give an account of those who love them.”41 In the same letter he reminds that if in those moments there was no joy and liveliness it is because there was no charity. It is for this that Superiors should always appear like fathers: “who love what the youth like, and the youth love what pleases the Superiors. In this way the work will be very bearable. The cause of the present change in the Oratory is that a good number of youth do not have confidence in the Superiors. Formerly all hearts were open to the Superiors, because of which the youth loved and obeyed promptly. But now the Superiors are considered only as such and not as fathers, brothers, friends.”42 Much to the contrary, “if we want to present ourselves as friends of the authentic good of all our students, if we want to oblige them to fulfill their duties, we should never forget that we represent the parents of these beloved youth…”43 It is the same for the religious.

Because of this, the Superiors must be those tried in virtue and possessed of a great charity: “Those in charge of this Oratory, since all exercise the title of charity, should fulfill it for each with zeal, since it is a tribute that lends itself to the divine Majesty; therefore they should all mutually encourage one another to persevere in their respective positions and to fulfill their duties conscientiously.”44

Your presence should be seen only as that of a father concerned for his children. Therefore better than words are deeds that move, and thus: “the Superior must be all things for all people, always ready to listen to every doubt or lament of the youth, all eyes to paternally watch over his conduct, all heart to seek the spiritual good of his subordinates and the temporal welfare of those whom providence has entrusted to his care.”45

If this love reigns, punishments are not necessary since those who have to obey have the same mind as the superiors in love. In those moved by love, there is no room for fear, since there is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; for fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not reached perfection in love (Jn 4:18). And when punishment is necessary, they themselves see the necessity of this punishment and the benefit meant by it.46 Still, when punishing we must show the love of Mothers, showing to them in it that we seek their good, and thus what Don Bosco teaches is perfectly applicable to the religious: “If then you have been true fathers of your students, it is because you have the hearts of fathers and never use repression and punishment without reason, without justice, but only as one who resigns himself to it by necessity and to fulfill a painful duty.”47 For this reason the Superiors must try to make them love more than fear, since by charity the most obstinate and rebellious hearts yield: “charity and patience accompany you faithfully when you order and when you correct, and work with such fortune that all know by your deeds and words that you seek the good of souls.”48 “Try, then, to attract them with love, moderation, or charity, not with arrogance or harshness, having with them the kindness that is suitable for every spiritual mother, according to the words of Our Lord: “Learn from Me for I am meek and humble of heart” (Mt. 11:29), imitating God of Whom we read: He disposed all things gently, avoiding principally imposing with violence our authority: God, in effect, has given us all freedom, and for this, he does not force anyone, but limits Himself to showing, to persuading. Sometimes, nevertheless, it will be necessary to act with authority and severity, when it is reasonably required by the circumstances and personal needs, but even in this case, the only thing that must move us in charity and zeal for souls.”49

Just as the soul behaves in the first act, principle of all the vital movements of man, by which we live, feel, and understand, so must be charity in the spiritual life: the first act, the principle by which all works are accomplished: “love is formally the life of the soul, like the soul is the life of the body.”50 Love should be the life of the soul in such a way that the activities and all works be carried out are ordered to God, since all done in the spirit of charity does not seek anything other than His greater glory.

Article 6: Environment of Family

In the Letter on the Spirit of Family, Don Bosco shows how the Oratory was no longer what it was before; it had neither joy nor liveliness because it did not have charity. And the cause of all this change, including in what was religious, was because there was no trust between the Superiors and the youth, that is to say, because there was not familiarity: “the cause of the present change in the Oratory is that a good number of the youth do not trust the Superiors. Once hearts were open to the Superiors, and because of this the youth loved and obeyed promptly. But now the Superiors are considered only as such, not as fathers, brothers, and friends; therefore they are more feared than loved.”51

The solution is in breaking this distrust with true family spirit that has to live in the Oratory, which must be like the extension of a good family in which the youth grow: “familiarity with the youth, especially in recreation. Without familiarity, affection cannot be demonstrated and without this demonstration there cannot be trust. He that wishes to be loved must demonstrate that he loves. Jesus Christ became little like the little ones and bore our infirmities. Here is the teacher of familiarity!”52

Only in the spirit of family, only in the spirit of trust that exists between parents, children, and siblings can the educative, religious, open to all, charitable, joyful and free environment live: “He that knows he is loved, loves, and he that is loved obtains all, especially from the youth. This trust establishes itself like an electric current between youth and Superiors. Hearts open and make known their needs and manifest their defects. This love makes it so the Superiors can bear the fatigues, dislikes, ingratitude, lack of discipline, flippancy, and negligence of the youth. Jesus Christ did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick. Here we have our model. Then there will not be one who works for vainglory; nor one who punishes to avenge his offended self-love; nor one who withdraws from the field of service for fear that others will have predominance; nor one who gossips about others to be loved and esteemed by the youth, to the exclusion of the other Superiors…; nor those who because of love of their own comfort, scorns the duty of attendance; nor those who for false human respect abstain from admonishing those who need to be admonished. If this effective love exists, it will not look for anything more than the glory of God and the good of souls.”53

Charity and patience are recommended to be practiced by all towards one another so as to bear each other's defects, and that it be preferred to fasts and penances.54 The charity of those who order and the charity of those who obey should make an environment like that of the little family of Nazareth reign, where there was no place for rumors, anger, sadness, envy, conflicts, or quarrels proper to those who do not have the spirit of Christ. If there is someone who is not disposed to live in this way, he should be removed from the Oratory, since being in it, he is not of it: “charity and patience with one another in order to bear with the defects of others, to promote the good reputation of the Oratory, of those in charge, and to encourage all to esteem and trust the Rector, are things that are insistently recommended to all; without them we will not succeed in maintaining order or in advancing the glory or God and the good of souls.55

Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory

Following in the footsteps of Don Bosco, regarding the Oratory, we must see the creative genius who knew well the different situations of the youth and gave them an adequate answer moved by an eminent pastoral charity.

Because of this we must know how to be docile and creative, resolute and reflective at the same time. We should how to be attentive to the situations of our time: “it is necessary to try to know our time and adapt ourselves to it.”56

We must return to the spirit the oratory had in the time of its creator since it should be “a house for those who lack one…”

Don Bosco uses these pastoral categories referring to other enterprises: “I propose to enter their houses...bring them to church (parish)...sit next to them in school...be their friend during the hours of recreation.”57

To grasp in depth that which an authentic Oratory should be – or to form our activities according to the spirit of the Oratory – means to know how to constantly adapt the works and activities to the condition of the youth and to the cultural transformations that shake the world of the youth.58 That is to say, to be docile to the will of the Lord and to the mission received of transmitting the Gospel, especially to the youth. And this search should be holy and enthusiastic (santamente apasionada).

Part II: The Oratorian Spirit

Now we will treat of the Oratory in its broad sense, that which we can call “the oratorian spirit.”

Chapter 1: Places and Times

Article 1: The Family

In this sense we consider that the “first Oratory” should be the family. Every good family should see that the children do not have idle hours, but that they amuse themselves virtuously, after having completed their daily duties, and on feast days, their religious duties.

Article 2: The School

The high schools, elementary and middle schools, etc. that are like a second home, should stand out because of its oratorian spirit, forming “good Christians and honest citizens.”59

Article 3: The Religious Communities

Each community of our little Religious Family also should live this spirit of healthy recreation and contagious joy, founded on the fulfillment of religious duties. Consider always that “God is the first served.”60

Article 4: Popular Missions

It is also the spirit that must live in the popular missions, especially in the Children's and Youth Misssions, but also, in its own way, in the other forms of mission.

Article 5: Houses of Formation

In a special way this oratorian spirit should live in our aspirancies, postulancies, novitiates, and juniorates. It lives when in these the first place, the most important, is give to God and to His Kingdom.61 It lives when it works, taking advantage of the present time (Eph 5:16; Col 4:5), in its educative, religious, and all-embracing environment, an environment of joy and freedom, of charity, and of true family.

Article 6: Intense Times of Rest

Likewise this oratorian spirit should live in the times of rest or recreation like: convivencias, camps, field trips, outings, conferences, congresses, floral games, etc.

For example, for us it is inconceivable for us to organize camps that are not “schools of life,” that is to say, without discipline, without a strong religious mark. Usually we organize them with two intense periods of prayer: in the morning, Holy Mass; in the afternoon, Eucharistic Adoration, or the Rosary if they are laity. At night, give them “good nights.” This simple plan works for all the other activities.

Chapter 2: Applications of the Oratorian Spirit

Finally, we consider that this oratorian environment, climate, or spirituality is nothing other than the expression of our spirituality “of the Incarnate Word” in concrete environments. At its roots, it is nothing other than the prolongation of a good Catholic family in these environments.

In other words, similar to the Christian family, the oratorian spirit is like a “spiritual womb.” Just as the family is a community of persons in love, a communion in love, so our houses must be communities of charity, to the point that one could say that in them lives Christ Himself.62

We consider that this oratorian spirit, in order to be molded of our spirituality, should be lived principally in the families from where it is extracted as way of life, in religious communities, in our schools, in seminaries, in times of rest, and finally in festive or daily oratories in imitation of Don Bosco.
